findings.source_quote: et ego sum pastor, et validissime oportet me de vobis reddere rationem.
findings.english_quote: I too am a shepherd, and I must give a most exacting account of you.
findings.issue: The emphatic validissime qualifies the obligation expressed by oportet. “Most exacting” instead characterizes the account, introducing a claim about its rigor while failing to locate the source's emphasis on the speaker's obligation.
findings.suggested_revision: Consider: “I too am a shepherd, and I am under the strongest obligation to give an account of you.” This proposal requires fresh review before adoption.

findings.source_quote: etenim licet quis eorum temptatus a nequissimo diabolo aliquid deliquerit, cito recurret ad dominum suum.
findings.english_quote: Even if the utterly wicked devil tempts one of them to do wrong, that person will quickly return to their Lord.
findings.issue: The selected Latin explicitly envisages someone committing an offense after being tempted. The simplified text makes temptation alone the concessive condition and omits the actual wrongdoing. This changes the difficult assertion about a quick return even after an offense.
findings.suggested_revision: Consider: “Even if one of them does wrong after being tempted by the utterly wicked devil, that person will quickly return to their Lord.” Review the replacement independently before adoption.

findings.source_quote: et ego sum pastor, et validissime oportet me de vobis reddere rationem.
findings.english_quote: I too am a shepherd. I must give a most exacting account of you.
findings.issue: As independently checked against the Latin, “most exacting” transfers the emphasis from the obligation to the character of the account. The source strongly emphasizes that the shepherd is obliged to account for the readers; it does not explicitly describe the account as exceptionally exacting.
findings.suggested_revision: Consider: “I too am a shepherd. I am under the strongest obligation to give an account of you.” The proposed simplified wording requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: dico autem omnibus vobis, quicumque sigillum hoc accepistis, simplicitatem habere neque offensarum memores esse neque in malitia vestra permanere aut in memoria offensarum amaritudinis, in unum quemque spiritum fieri et has malas scissuras permediare ac tollere a vobis, ut dominus pecorum gaudeat de his.
findings.english_quote: Shorter sentences preserve the shepherd’s authority, ethical scope, blood-guilt and remedy language, and all noted alternatives.
findings.issue: The simplification metadata claims preservation of “blood-guilt” language, but this selected unit contains no blood-guilt expression. Its offenses, wickedness, bitterness, and divisions must not be relabeled as an explicit blood-guilt claim.
findings.suggested_revision: Remove “blood-guilt” from this unit's simplification rationale. Describe the actual source content, such as ethical instructions, divisions, and their removal, without importing terminology from another passage.

summary: Both editions require revision after separate clause-by-clause review against the selected Latin. The standard covers the clauses but misplaces the final emphasis on obligation. The simplified edition additionally omits actual wrongdoing from the concessive promise and contains inaccurate blood-guilt metadata. Both retain the necessity of entering the kingdom, the restricted no-one-will-perish assertion, speaker attribution, and contextual repentance terminology. The notes distinguish bracketed [pro] as editorial supply and frame witness comparisons as reported or edition-mediated; no source change is required merely because alternatives exist. This review does not authenticate unseen images, certify editions or handwriting, or establish exhaustive collation. All proposed replacements remain subject to fresh review.
